courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
md: 3DGS trades memory for speed: hundreds of megabytes of explicit parameters instead of a few megabytes of network weights, in exchange for rendering at well over 30 FPS and training in tens of minutes.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Removing a stage is not always a clean subtraction. You must decide what replaces it: no rewrite at all, or a trivial rewrite; BM25 alone, or BM25 with more candidates to keep the reranker's input size equal. State the replacement, because different choices give different deltas.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: IDOR and BOLA: changing one number in the URL
md: The OWASP API Security Top 10 warns that comparing the session's user id with an id parameter covers only a small subset of BOLA cases. Objects are often shared (a team folder, a manager viewing a report), so the real question is "may this user perform this action on this object under our policy", which lessons 11 and 12 turn into one reusable check.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Enforce authorization in one place: deny by default, policy engines
md: Central does not mean single. Next.js apps that checked access only in middleware were exposed when CVE-2025-29927 let requests skip middleware (lesson 7). Decide policy in one place, but enforce it at more than one layer: at the route, and again at the data (scoped queries, RLS).

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Moving a service account to AES is not a fix by itself. An AES ticket for `Summer2019!` is still crackable; it only costs more per guess. The fix is a password nobody can guess: a gMSA or a long random secret.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AD CS: when a certificate template hands out admin
md: In AD a certificate trusted for client authentication is a password that survives password resets. ESC1 is a template that lets any user choose the name in the certificate. Audit templates, treat CAs as Tier 0, watch 4886 and 4887 for mismatched subjects, and revoke rather than reset.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: OOXML: a zip of XML parts, and links that fetch remote content
md: A document can be dangerous with zero bytes of code inside it. In OOXML, read every .rels part: one line with TargetMode External can be the whole attack.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Anti-debugging and anti-VM: recognising checks and getting past them
md: An empty sandbox report means 'not observed in this environment', never 'benign'. Say exactly that in your notes and in any verdict you hand to the SOC.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
md: A format string bug is a primitive factory: the read directives leak, and %n writes. The cure is structural and cheap: constant format strings, enforced by -Werror=format-security and static analysis.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: OPSEC through the defender's eyes: every action leaves a trace
md: Map each emulated step to the log that must record it before the exercise. If the step passes unseen, the gap is in one of three places: the data was never collected, it was collected but no rule looked, or a rule fired and nobody acted. Lesson 12 names these gaps.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: Outcome grading is not the same as correct behavior. A grader only sees what it checks: tests that cover one interpretation, a database diff, an answer string. Anything outside the check (rudeness, a policy step skipped, an unrelated file deleted) can pass silently.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
md: Compaction is lossy. The Agent SDK docs warn that specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive a summary. Put durable rules in a file that is re-injected on every request (the SDK uses CLAUDE.md for this), not only in the first user message.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: EchoLeak: one email, zero clicks, Copilot leaks
md: Every one of Microsoft's controls existed and every one had a gap. Layered defence only works if each layer is complete on its own: all Markdown syntaxes, all allowlisted domains, all retrieval paths.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Misinformation and unbounded consumption
md: Agents multiply consumption: one user request can trigger many model calls and tool calls in a loop. Cap steps per task and total tokens per task, not only per request, or a confused agent (or an injected one) can run until the budget is gone.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: A generator's novelty number is only as good as its reference set and structure matcher. Note that the same disorder issue from the GNoME critique appears here: the synthesized TaCr2O6 was disordered, and MatterGen's ordered-disordered matcher exists so that an ordered variant of a known disordered compound is not counted as new.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Green lists shift probabilities toward a keyed subset (distortionary). Gumbel sampling and two-competitor tournaments keep each token's distribution exact and hide the signal in correlations between chosen tokens and keyed random values. All of them need entropy to work.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Workflow: capture once with an interposer, analyze with a heap profiler to find what to fix in code, convert to a workload, then replay that one workload against each allocator or tuning and compare RSS against ideal RSS.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: For time series, first remove what is predictable (seasonality and level), then apply a robust score to the residual. The detector is only as good as the baseline: a residual is anomalous relative to a model of normal for that moment.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: OAuth is about **authorization**: letting a client act on a user's behalf with limited scope. The access token is meant for the resource server, not for the client to learn who the user is. Logging users in needs OpenID Connect (lesson 10).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Misconception: "we validate the token at the API gateway, so services can just decode it." Then any path around the gateway, and any token for another audience the gateway also accepts, reaches services that trust it blindly. Each service should at least check the audience meant for it.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: What an application security programme is, and who owns what
md: "Security owns security" is the most common misconception. A central team that tries to fix everything becomes a bottleneck and then gets bypassed. The working model: developers own fixes, the security team owns the system that makes fixes happen.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Testing the running app: DAST, IAST, SCA recall and fuzzing in CI
md: No method sees everything. SAST and SCA see code and dependencies early; DAST sees the deployed surface; IAST sees runtime paths the tests exercise; fuzzing sees parsers under abuse. Pick by what your application does: an API with a heavy parser needs fuzzing more than a static brochure site does.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Metrics that matter: time to remediate, open age and coverage
md: Measure what is still open and what you cannot see. Mean time to remediate, open age, SLA compliance and coverage together describe a programme; any one alone can be gamed by accident.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Misconception: *a text's embedding is a fixed property of the text.* In a role-aware model the same string gets one vector as a query and a different vector as a document, by design. Which vector you get depends on how you called the model.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
md: Do not cache or replay a 429 as if it were an answer. RFC 6585 says responses with status 429 "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". Also note that a 429 is not always temporary: Anthropic returns 429 without a `retry-after` header when an organization reaches its monthly spend cap, and retrying keeps failing until access resumes.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: `volatile` does not fix this. In C and C++ it stops the compiler from removing or reordering accesses within one thread, which suits signal handlers and memory-mapped I/O, but cppreference states it is not suitable for communication between threads. A volatile `counter++` is still a separate read and write.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Mean pooling suits sounds that last (rain, engine hum, music) and resists one-patch glitches. Max pooling catches short events (a bark, a door slam, a gunshot) but turns any single false patch into a clip-level false alarm. PANNs combines both inside the network: its global pooling sums the time-averaged and the time-maximized feature vectors.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id and cost parameters
md: Store passwords with Argon2id (or scrypt, or bcrypt for legacy), a unique salt per user, and a cost tuned as high as your login traffic allows. Record the parameters with each hash, and raise them over time.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Passkeys and WebAuthn: why phishing stops working
md: Passkeys resist phishing because the browser binds every signature to the real site's origin and the credential to the site's domain. The user's judgment is not part of the security argument.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: Converse unifies the **shape** of requests and responses, not the **behavior** of models. Models still differ in quality, context length, supported content types and tool support, which the docs list per model. A one-line modelId swap is easy; validating that the new model is good enough is still your job.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Rust binaries: mangled paths, slices and panics
md: In Rust binaries, follow the panics. Every `panic_bounds_check`, `unwrap` failure and `expect` message carries a source location or message string. Even when symbols are stripped, cross-references to those strings map functions back to files and lines in the original crate.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
md: Why activations stay at 8 bits: per-token absmax gives the largest entry 127 levels, so a few outliers still leave room for the rest. At 4 bits (-8 to 7) one outlier squeezes most entries to 0. The BitNet team found the states before the FFN down projection the worst. BitNet a4.8 keeps those at 8 bits and sparsifies them; BitNet v2 rotates them with a Hadamard transform first (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: Speculation is not a correctness risk for your program: wrong-path results never reach registers or memory. It is only a time cost. (It can leak information through caches, which is the Spectre family of attacks; lesson 5 touches on that.)

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Firefox Fission and WebKit: the same idea, different shapes
md: Misconception: "every modern browser isolates every site." Coverage depends on product and device. Android WebView and low-memory Android have no site isolation in Chromium's documentation, and WebKit's is still being built. A risk assessment for an app that embeds web content must check the actual engine and platform.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: The patch gap: from upstream fix to every Chromium in every app
md: Misconception: "we run the latest Chrome, so we are patched." A typical laptop also runs several Electron apps (chat, editors, meeting clients), each with its own Chromium, plus WebViews inside mobile apps. Each has its own patch gap, and the attacker picks the slowest.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Leveled: low space and read amplification, high write amplification. Tiered: low write amplification, more runs to read and up to about 2x temporary space during a full merge. The size ratio T slides each policy along its curve.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Resilience, continuity and recovery: the words and the plans
md: A disaster recovery plan is not a business continuity plan. The DRP brings systems back at another site; the BCP keeps the business working while they are gone, often by hand. Maersk staff booked containers through WhatsApp and personal Gmail during NotPetya: that was continuity without systems, improvised because it was not planned.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups nobody restored: monitoring and testing that prove recovery
md: A green backup dashboard measures jobs, not recovery. Measure what a restore needs: the latest *verified restorable* point (your real RPO) and the last measured restore time at full size (your real RTO). Restore time grows with data size, so a test on last year's volume says little about today's.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When recovery tools fail too: CrowdStrike 2024, keys and break-glass
md: A recovery key stored only inside the thing it recovers is not a recovery key. The same goes for admin passwords in a vault that runs on the failed platform, runbooks on the wiki that is down, and an on-call rota in the chat tool that is offline.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Bytes remove the vocabulary and its blind spots, but multiply the number of positions by roughly 4. Since compute is about $2mT$, a byte model is only practical if the big network runs on far fewer positions than there are bytes.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Byte models trade a tokenizer for an extra design choice: how to group bytes. With learned, entropy-based patches, BLT matched BPE models at 8B for equal training FLOPs, improved robustness and spelling, and turned patch size into a knob that trades steps for model size.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: Audit unsafe code at the module boundary. Keep fields that unsafe code trusts private, check every invariant before the unsafe block (as `assert!(mid <= len)` does), and write a SAFETY comment that names the invariant.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: Arrange data so that what you use together sits together, and walk it in address order. Stride 1 is the cheapest pattern there is.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a transformer as circuits: residual paths, QK and OV
md: A head is two circuits. QK, built from $W_Q^\top W_K$, picks where to look; OV, built from $W_O W_V$, picks what to copy. With patterns frozen, the whole model is a sum of linear paths through OV and residual connections.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: A low CTR at rank 4 does not mean a document is less relevant than one at rank 1. CTR mixes two things: how often the slot is seen and how good the document is. You must separate them before clicks can serve as relevance labels.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stored XSS and the worms it made: Samy and TweetDeck
md: Both worms are stored XSS that spread because the payload could use the victim's session to store itself again. Both trace back to a gap in **output encoding**: a filter that guessed at browser parsing (MySpace) and one rendering path that skipped escaping (TweetDeck). Encoding has to happen on every path, as the very last step before data enters HTML.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Why CLIP learns from captions instead of fixed labels
md: CLIP does not learn to describe images. It learns two encoders whose outputs agree: a matching image and caption land close together in one shared vector space, and non-matching ones land apart. Everything else in this course (zero-shot classification, retrieval, the failure modes) follows from that geometry.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Blind spots: data events, flow logs and traffic you never see
md: Misconception: "VPC Flow Logs record every packet on the network". They record summaries per flow, aggregated over up to 10 minutes by default (1 minute on Nitro instances), and they skip whole categories of traffic, including the instance metadata service and Amazon DNS.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Snowflake 2024 and SaaS platforms: hunting from the customer's side
md: Misconception: "the vendor was not breached, so this is the vendor's problem". In both Snowflake 2024 and Salesloft Drift 2025, the evidence, the containment levers (users, network policies, tokens, secrets) and the exposure decision sat with each customer.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Serverless: execution roles, event injection and function secrets
md: Serverless removes servers, not responsibility. A function is code plus a role plus its triggers: validate every event as untrusted input, give each function only the role it needs, and keep secrets in a secret store rather than in configuration.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: How AWS decides: explicit deny, SCPs, boundaries and resource policies
md: "We added an Allow, so it should work" is the classic debugging trap. If anything anywhere has a matching `Deny`, including an SCP you cannot see from inside the account, no Allow will help. AWS's documentation advises asking your organization's administrators when an SCP might be the cause.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Incident response for a leaked cloud key
md: For a leaked key: deactivate first, then investigate with CloudTrail across all Regions, then hunt for persistence (new users, keys, roles and policies) before declaring it closed. Then remove the reason a long-lived key existed at all.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Agglomerative clustering: linkages and the dendrogram
md: The scikit-learn guide warns that agglomerative clustering has a "rich get richer" behaviour that leads to uneven cluster sizes, with single linkage the worst and Ward the most regular. Its linkage comparison example adds that single linkage "performs poorly in the presence of noise" while Ward is "the most effective method for noisy data".

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: A selection vector is not a filtered copy. Downstream primitives read the original vectors at the listed positions. That avoids copying, but the reads are now indirect and sparse, which matters for SIMD (next lesson).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
md: Vectorization processes several elements per instruction, but only when the compiler can prove it is safe: known trip counts and non-overlapping pointers help. -O2 in GCC vectorizes only the easy cases (no runtime checks, and before GCC 15 no epilogue); -O3 also takes loops that need runtime alias checks.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Measure it: benchmarking builds and an end-to-end tuning run
md: Misconception: "fewer instructions or higher IPC means faster." Here -O0 had the best IPC and the worst time, and -O2 versus -O3 showed a 60 ms median gap with identical instructions. Time is the result; instructions, IPC and cache misses are clues that explain it.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: An atomic load followed by an atomic store is **not** an atomic read-modify-write. The fix here is `num.fetch_add(1, AcqRel)`, which makes L and S one indivisible step. Atomics remove data races; they do not remove race conditions in your logic.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Why one big ODE step from noise collapses to the mean
md: A diffusion model knows the *local* direction at each point. One-step generation needs the *global* answer: where does the whole trajectory end? A consistency model learns that endpoint directly.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: The goal of consistent hashing: when the set of servers changes, move only the keys that must move, which is about $K/N$ keys for $K$ keys and $N$ servers, and never shuffle keys between servers that did not change.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
md: A missing field scores **1**, the best possible decay value, in both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Profiles with no location beat everyone who lives a few kilometers away. Decide explicitly: require the field with an `exists` filter (it keeps only documents that have a value in that field), index a default value, or accept the behavior on purpose.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: A solver turns a declarative model into search plus propagation plus learning. Your job is the model: tight domains, global constraints instead of many small ones, integer scaling, and a time limit with a status check.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
md: Misconception: "runAsNonRoot is enough". It stops UID 0, but a non-root process with `allowPrivilegeEscalation` left at its default of true can still become root through a setuid binary in the image. Set both, and drop capabilities.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
md: Label every namespace with a Pod Security level: Restricted for applications, Baseline at minimum, Privileged only for reviewed system namespaces. Add a policy engine for rules PSA cannot express, and treat its webhook as critical infrastructure.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
md: Use both views: the audit log for who changed what through the API, and a syscall-level sensor such as Falco for what processes actually do. Each covers the other's blind spot.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Strict mode guarantees the diff is **schema-valid**, not that it is **right**. A perfectly typed `{"remove": []}` for *drop the salary limit* is still a wrong state. Schema enforcement removes parsing failures; only evaluation (lesson 6) catches meaning failures.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Faithfulness is a causal claim about what drove the answer. You test it by intervening, not by reading. A biasing feature that flips answers without ever being mentioned proves the CoT omitted a real cause.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Building and scoring a CoT monitor
md: Misconception: "our monitor has an AUROC of 0.95, so it is good enough." AUROC averages recall over all false-positive rates, including ones no review team could handle. Report recall at the FPR you will actually run, and precision at a realistic base rate.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A bi-encoder pays the document cost once, offline. A cross-encoder pays the full transformer cost for every (query, document) pair at query time. That single fact explains both why it is more accurate and why it can only rerank a shortlist.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Misconception: "nobody knows our format, so it is safe". That is security through obscurity. Formats leak, binaries get reverse-engineered, employees leave. If learning the algorithm breaks your system, it was never secure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
md: Do not use one key for two jobs (say, encryption and MAC, or client-to-server and server-to-client). Derive separate keys with HKDF and distinct labels.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Nonce budgets for AEAD: counters, random nonces, XChaCha, GCM-SIV
md: "Each server picks random nonces, so we are fine" is only true while the total across all servers stays under the cap. Ten servers each sending a billion messages a year under one key pass 2^32 in under six months. Count per key, not per server.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Reviewing crypto code: safe APIs, tests and migration
md: Prefer APIs that remove choices, pin every parameter to the key, test that misuse is rejected, and keep an inventory so that when an algorithm, library or key fails, you know exactly what to rotate.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: More stages are not automatically faster. Each stage costs shared memory that a bigger tile or an epilogue staged through shared memory could use, and once loads are hidden, extra stages add nothing. StageCountAuto simply fills what is left.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: From device to NUMA node: decoders, interleaving and regions
md: Pick the memory zone deliberately. Hot-plugged CXL memory can be onlined as `ZONE_MOVABLE` or `ZONE_NORMAL`. Kernel allocations are generally not migratable and can only use `ZONE_NORMAL` or lower, so CXL memory in `ZONE_MOVABLE` serves only user pages and other movable data. `daxctl` onlines as movable by default; that keeps kernel data off the device but means CXL capacity cannot absorb kernel memory pressure.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
md: Reading what a server sends you is not breaking in, but laws differ by state and country, and accusations can come anyway. Collect the minimum to prove a flaw, report it privately, keep records, and wait for the fix.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
md: DMCA 1201 bans circumventing access controls on copyrighted works even without copying; the security research exemption (renewed every three years) covers good-faith research on devices you lawfully own, but not other laws or tool trafficking. Trade secret law cares about where your copy of a secret came from.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
md: ISC2: four canons, enforced through certification. ACM: avoid harm, respect privacy, report risks, access only when authorised. Menlo: respect for persons, beneficence, justice, respect for law and public interest. Ask before you experiment on people, including code reviewers.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
md: A learned weight is a share of a budget, not a property of the domain. Copying published weights to a run 10 times longer silently multiplies every domain's epochs by 10. Always convert weights to epochs for your own budget and data sizes before training.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: SoA is not automatically faster. Its advantage is exactly the fraction of each record that a loop does *not* touch. A loop that uses every field gains nothing from the layout change, and some access patterns get worse (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
md: A match is evidence, not proof. Pattern plus checksum gives low confidence; only context (keywords, expiry dates, nearby names) raises it. Tune discovery and DLP rules to act on high confidence and review the low-confidence bucket, rather than blocking on every 16-digit number.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security II: auditing reads and the Snowflake thefts
md: Log reads of restricted data, not just changes: pgAudit object logging on sensitive columns, warehouse query history, cloud data events. Alert on sequences (list everything, stage, export, download) and on volume compared with the same account's normal.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: An alarm nobody should trip: why deception detects
md: Deception is not "hacking back" or trapping people into crimes. Decoys sit inside your own systems and only watch. What you may do with what they record is covered in lesson 12.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Placement and the deception story: where decoys earn their keep
md: Count matters less than plausibility and position. A few decoys that fit your naming scheme and sit where credentials and maps lead will outperform many generic ones.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
md: To find rare bugs, maximize the *diversity* of runs, not the intensity of each one. Random per-run choices of faults, features and buggify sites cover far more distinct states than one heavily tuned configuration.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
md: The most dangerous line in a plan is often not an open port but a `-/+` or `-` on something stateful: a database, a bucket, a KMS key. Replacements are triggered by innocent-looking edits (a renamed resource, a changed engine version), and a reviewer skimming for security groups will miss them.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
md: Three edits turn a GPT into a masked diffusion LM: a [MASK] id, `is_causal=False`, and targets at the same positions as the inputs. In practice add a fourth, relative positions such as RoPE, so the bidirectional model learns locality quickly. At equal size and steps it trains to a worse likelihood than the GPT, and its samples get better as each pass commits fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
md: Scaling or admitting on the current load of the other pool oscillates. Mooncake saw it with early rejection: decode looks idle, so many requests are admitted; they reach decode one prefill later, decode looks full, so admissions stop and prefill idles, and the cycle repeats in opposite phase. Its fix was to decide on the decode load predicted for when the request will arrive there.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
md: These artefacts show that a *user account* interacted with a file, a folder or a drive. They are strongest together and with the drive in hand.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
md: Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: Turning a pair into one desirable and one undesirable example, as the paper does to compare against DPO, is described by its authors as a naive assumption: a chosen answer is only better than its sibling, not necessarily good.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Not every mismatch is a bug in the new store. If the new store is fed asynchronously, from a queue or a CDC stream, it is eventually consistent with the old one: a read right after a write can compare a fresh control with a candidate that is milliseconds behind. Measure that lag, and only `ignore` such cases after confirming they converge.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Common misconception: "eBPF is safe, so tracing can't hurt production." The verifier guarantees the kernel won't crash or hang, but it does not bound *how often* your program runs. A kprobe on a function called millions of times per second can still cost a large fraction of every CPU.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Why appliances are hard to defend: patches, logs and trust
md: Treat an appliance as a server you cannot see into. Get its logs out as they are written, limit the secrets it holds, and plan in advance for the day you must rebuild it.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Detecting a compromised appliance from the outside
md: When you cannot see inside a device, watch its edges: every connection it starts, every session that changes address, every account that uses it, and every configuration change. Those records live on other systems the intruder does not control.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
md: A length term changes which correct answers GRPO reinforces most. Without it, all correct answers in a group are equal; with it, the shortest correct one gets the largest advantage.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing
md: Deciding whether to think is often a bigger lever than shortening the thinking. Evaluate every option, from NoThinking to full thinking, on an accuracy-versus-tokens frontier per difficulty level, and check whether accuracy differences exceed the noise of your test set.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Case mapping and case folding: when lower() is not one-to-one
md: Locale-aware case mapping makes it worse: in Turkish, `I` lower-cases to dotless ı. Code that lower-cases with the server's locale can give different answers on different machines. For identifiers, use locale-independent case folding, as Python's `str.casefold()` is.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Polyglot files, content sniffing and LangSec
md: Checking the first bytes of an upload is not validation. A file can carry one format's signature and another format's content. If a file must be an image, decode it with an image library and re-encode it to a fresh file; whatever was hidden in it does not survive.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
md: Microsoft states AppLocker is "a defense-in-depth security feature and not considered a defensible Windows security feature": it does not meet Microsoft's servicing criteria, so a bypass is not treated as a vulnerability. Use it to raise the bar and to control what users run; use App Control for Business where you need a security boundary.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
md: Event-based methods need step changes. Hart's own NALM page lists three appliance classes: ON/OFF (bulbs, toasters), multi-state (washing machines, dishwashers with fill, rinse and spin states) and continuously variable (light dimmers, variable-speed tools). The last class is hard to monitor nonintrusively because it does not generate step changes in power.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: The independence assumption double-counts correlated fields. Company name and website domain usually agree or disagree together, so adding both full weights overstates the evidence. Merge strongly correlated fields into one comparison, or check calibration on labeled pairs: whether pairs scored 0.9 really match about 90% of the time.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: Count who can become Global Administrator, not only who is one: role assigners, admin credential resetters, app credential managers and hybrid identity admins. Keep the count small, make it eligible rather than active, and keep two tested emergency accounts outside it.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Entra access is a chain: a 60 to 90 minute access token renewed by a 90-day refresh token that is bound to user and client, not to a resource. Revocation cuts the chain; CAE cuts the current link at Exchange, SharePoint, Teams and Graph.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: A Conditional Access policy set is only as strong as what it does not cover. Inventory the exclusions, the service principals and the allowed flows, block legacy authentication and device code, and test every change in report-only mode first.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
md: Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: Common misconception: "the binary has every mitigation enabled, so this overflow is not a security issue." Every mitigation in this course has a known bypass class (lesson 14), and real exploits combine several bugs to get past them. An overflow is a security bug whether or not today's exploit techniques reach it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer (a race detector such as ThreadSanitizer, which flags conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory) to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt
md: Compression is lossy, and lossy is only safe when it is **unbiased**. Probabilistic quantization and scaled subsampling are unbiased per client, so their errors average out across a round. A biased compressor (rounding to nearest, keeping only the largest entries) pushes every client the same way, which looks like drift in disguise.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
md: Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Build it: a DeepSeekMoE layer with bias balancing in your GPT
md: Do not read quality conclusions off a run this small. Character-level Shakespeare with a 3.65M-parameter MoE (0.9M active) trains in under an hour per run on a CPU; differences of a few thousandths in validation loss between configurations are within seed noise. What this lab shows reliably is the mechanism: what the router does without balancing, and how each method changes the expert loads.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Case: Baton Drop and BlackLotus, a signed door left open
md: "Fixed" and "no longer trusted" are different states. Until the vulnerable signed binary is revoked or rolled past, the fix protects only machines whose attacker politely uses the new file.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-2 kernel tile by tile: forward, backward, parallelism
md: Every later kernel is this loop. FlashAttention-3's producer warps load $K_j, V_j$ and its pipeline overlaps the next $S_{ij}$ with the current $PV$; FlashAttention-4 moves $S$ and $P$ out of registers into a new on-chip memory, pairs thread blocks for the five backward matmuls, and orders causal tiles longest first (lessons 6 to 8). Only the mapping onto hardware changes.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Generating data by following a velocity field from noise
md: A flow model is a learned velocity field plus an ODE solver. Flow matching makes the *training* of that field as cheap as regression; the *sampling* cost is the number of solver steps.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
md: Checking ISpec with TLC is complete only for the model you configured. A passing inductive check at 3 acceptors is strong evidence, not a proof for 7; the TLAPS proof is what removes the bound.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
md: Match the tool to the question. Is the design right? Model check it. Must it hold for every size? Prove the design. Does the code do what the design says? Prove refinement, or validate traces. Is this function free of panics and overflow? Model check or prove the code. Each answer covers only what it was asked.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: When low precision fails: outliers, SwiGLU and debugging a run
md: Do not trust a short run. Fishman et al.'s divergence appeared after about 200B tokens, twice the length of earlier FP8 studies, and Lee et al. expect their own short runs underestimate instability. A recipe that matches BF16 for a few billion tokens has only passed the easy part.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Bots in business flows: ticket scalping and the BOTS Act
md: Limits that count per account are limits per fake account. Count against every scarce identifier an order carries, and decide who may enter before the rush, not during it.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Finding rings with graphs: shared devices, cards and addresses
md: Fraud hides in groups. Link accounts by rare shared identifiers, drop identifiers that honest crowds share, and review dense components rather than single accounts.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
md: A score is only a probability if it is calibrated. Raw scores from many models are not; a "0.8" may mean 30% fraud. Calibrate on recent labelled data before you plug scores into expected-cost thresholds.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Adaptive adversaries: shadow mode, response and running the programme
md: Every control has a half-life. Launch in shadow mode, watch for adaptation through volume and loss metrics, run large attacks as incidents, and keep an inventory of every flow an attacker could farm.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: On macOS, Apple's Xcode clang ships without libFuzzer (the Atheris documentation says the same), and Homebrew's clang needs the SDK path (`-isysroot $(xcrun --show-sdk-path)`) to find system headers. On Linux, distribution clang packages include it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: The Broadcom case was found by reverse engineering and code review, not fuzzing, and its lesson for fuzzers is about reach: the dangerous code ran only for specific frame types in specific connection states. A stateless fuzzer of single frames would rarely get there.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: Geometric hashing moves the expensive work offline: every model is stored under every basis. At query time one correct scene basis is enough, and it never needs to know in advance which model point it corresponds to.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
md: A shared geohash prefix guarantees closeness: both points are inside the same cell. The reverse is false: two points can be meters apart and share no prefix, because they straddle a cell boundary. Every correct proximity search must look at neighboring cells, not just one prefix.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: A caching allocator turns slow, synchronizing driver calls into fast CPU-side bookkeeping. The price is that freed memory is *kept*, so reserved memory, not allocated memory, is what other processes on the GPU see.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
md: All of these allocators are the same pattern at different layers: grab big memory rarely, carve it with your own rules, and choose block sizes that match the workload. Equal sizes kill external fragmentation; growable virtual ranges kill slivers; stream order makes reuse cheap.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: These measurements come from older GPUs (Fermi and Kepler in the post, Volta in the guide). Absolute numbers on a current GPU will differ, and larger caches can hide some waste. The sector and bank rules they illustrate are the ones the current CUDA guides still document.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: Rank by gap times time share, with an attainable target instead of 100 percent. The biggest gap and the biggest win are usually different kernels, and a gap on a kernel with a small time share is never worth a rewrite.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG is not a better retriever for every question. For a specific fact ("Who supplies Rover X2 motors?") plain vector RAG already finds c2, and the paper itself shows vector RAG gives the most *direct* answers. GraphRAG's measured gains are on broad sensemaking questions, the ones that need an understanding of the whole corpus.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Graph RAG variants differ in where they spend LLM calls: GraphRAG spends heavily at indexing (extraction, summaries, reports) and on map calls per global query; FastGraphRAG cuts extraction; LightRAG drops communities; HippoRAG drops summaries and lets PPR do the multi-hop work.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: RLOO, GSPO, off-policy drift, and what RLVR teaches
md: Before trusting an RLVR gain: test on several model families (a Qwen-only result may be amplified priors), compare against random and format-only rewards, and compare against distilling a stronger model (lesson 6).

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Phone phreaking: when the voice line was also the control line
md: In-band signalling fails because whoever can send data can also send commands. The durable fix is to separate the control channel from the data channel so the attacker has no way to reach it. You will meet the same idea as parameterised SQL queries and as never evaluating text found inside log messages.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Code Red, Slammer and Blaster: worms faster than people
md: At internet speed, the defence has to be in place before the worm arrives: patches installed, unneeded services unreachable, firewalls on by default, and automatic updates for machines without an administrator. Human response time is measured in minutes; Slammer finished in about ten.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: SolarWinds and Log4Shell: what you install and what you import
md: A valid digital signature does not mean software is safe. It proves who published it and that it was not altered afterwards. If the attacker is inside the publisher's build, the malicious code is signed along with everything else, as with SolarWinds.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
md: A sound counter workflow: `perf stat` for IPC and TopdownL1, drill into the biggest bucket with grouped metrics, then `perf record` on the matching event with `:pp` to find the code, change it, and measure again.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: One request, two readers: why proxies and caches disagree
md: Every bug in this course is a **parser differential**: two programs read the same message and reach different conclusions. The durable fixes remove the room for disagreement (one unambiguous framing, one definition of the cache key) rather than trying to spot bad requests one by one.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: The 2025 endgame: 0.CL, Expect and upstream HTTP/1.1
md: The structural fix for request smuggling is to stop sending HTTP/1.1 between your own servers. Until then, every hop must reject ambiguous requests, and every code path must consume the body or close the connection.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a 2 MiB mapping: offset bits, alignment, contiguity
md: Misconception: "the box has 40 GiB free, so it can provide 40 GiB of huge pages." Huge pages need aligned, physically contiguous free runs. After fragmentation, requests can come up short or have to wait for compaction.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
md: The duality does not make Mamba-2 as good at recall as softmax attention. The quadratic form is a way to compute the same layer faster in training; at inference, all past information still has to pass through the fixed state, and there is no softmax to pick one token sharply.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
md: Fusion is about **recall of the shortlist** (the share of relevant documents that make it in); reranking is about **precision at the top** (the share of the top few that are relevant). Fused-list quality caps what the reranker can achieve, and rerank depth N trades latency for the chance to rescue documents fused low.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Zones and conduits: the ISA/IEC 62443 way to segment
md: A conduit is a promise in two parts: only these services, between only these zones. Write it down as a table, enforce it with firewalls or gateways, and monitor it so that anything outside the table becomes an alert.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon
md: CISA's 2025 primary mitigations for OT read like a summary of these four cases: remove OT connections to the public internet, change default passwords, secure remote access, segment IT and OT, and practise operating manually.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: XML Signature from zero: canonical form, digests and SignedInfo
md: The W3C specification's security section says it in two lines: *only what is signed is secure*, and applications should *see what is signed*, meaning they must act on the exact data that was hashed and verified, not on some other view of the document.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: SCIM provisioning: creating and removing accounts in every app
md: Deprovisioning is more than `active: false`. A leaver's access also lives in open sessions, refresh tokens, personal API keys and OAuth grants the user created inside the app. Check what your apps do on SCIM deactivation; if the answer is "only blocks the next login", add the rest to the offboarding runbook.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Joiner, mover, leaver: the lifecycle and how access creeps
md: Compute access from the authoritative record (desired state) and apply the difference both ways. Movers are the riskiest event, because add-only processes never remove anything.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Service accounts and non-human identities
md: Non-human identities have no leaving date, so give them an owner, an expiry and a last-used check. When a secret may be exposed, rotate all of them, including the ones you believe are unused: that belief is what Cloudflare's attacker used.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: A robust change detector is: align (features, RANSAC, homography, optional ECC refinement), mask invalid warped borders, correct photometry using pixels that probably did not change, difference, threshold (Otsu when the histogram is two-humped), then open the mask with a kernel smaller than the smallest change you care about.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Hashing evidence and keeping a chain of custody
md: Hash at collection, hash at every transfer, analyse only copies. A hash that matches the one recorded at acquisition is what lets you say "this is exactly what we took from the machine".

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: When the incident is not an attack: CrowdStrike, July 2024
md: Treat large non-malicious outages with the same machinery as attacks: incident commander, severity, OOB communications, a timeline and a blameless review. Attackers will use the confusion either way.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Shellshock: when an environment variable became code
md: Shellshock is injection into an interpreter nobody thought was in the path. The data (a header) was never concatenated into code by the application; the interpreter itself treated a data channel (the environment) as code. Know which interpreters your input reaches, including the ones your libraries start for you.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Inside a connected device: microcontrollers, flash and the boot ROM
md: Every protection in a device rests on something that cannot change: code in boot ROM and bits in OTP. Everything in flash can be updated, by the maker or by an attacker who gets write access. Good design decides early which checks and secrets go where.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Device vulnerability handling: disclosure, SBOMs and the CRA
md: Vulnerability handling is a pipeline: a published way to receive reports, an SBOM to find affected products, a signed update path to fix them, a stated support period, and (in the EU) 24-hour, 72-hour and final reports for exploited bugs. Missing any stage breaks the rest.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
md: A backtracking regex is dangerous when one string can be matched in many ways: a quantifier inside a quantifier, alternatives that overlap such as `(a|a)*`, or several `.*` in a row. The slow case is the near miss, so a test with matching strings will never show it. On Node.js the cost is paid by every user of the process.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Finding and catching JavaScript bugs: tools, signals, practice
md: One idea runs through the whole course: in JavaScript the boundaries you assume (an object, a context, a module, a header, a renderer) are usually not security boundaries. Real boundaries are processes, operating system users, origins and authenticated messages. Put untrusted input and untrusted code behind one of those, and check permission where the data is used.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
md: Linearizability checking is a search for one legal order inside the real-time constraints. Its cost is driven by how many operations overlap, so you control it by limiting operations per key and by turning known non-effects (like timed-out reads) into `:fail`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: Three defences, in order: prune what cannot run, search within a budget you chose from a convergence curve, and promote only wins that are larger than the noise. A tuner without the third one is a random walk through your performance history.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Why Windows trusts drivers: the kernel line and the admin line
md: Two separate questions decide whether kernel code runs: *who* asks (only admins may load drivers, and admin-to-kernel is not a serviced boundary) and *which code* it is (the signature check). Every defence in this course strengthens the second question, because on Windows the first one is already answered once an attacker is admin.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: VBS and memory integrity: taking code checks out of the kernel
md: Memory integrity protects kernel **code**, not kernel **data**. A BYOVD driver that lets a caller change kernel memory can still alter data structures in VTL0, such as callback registrations or policy variables, and memory integrity does not stop that. HVCI is necessary, not sufficient.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
md: Epilogue fusion matters less than elementwise fusion for big GEMMs: the matmul is compute bound and dominates, so removing a 66 us kernel from a 947 us layer saves about 7 percent. It matters more for small or skinny matmuls, where the GEMM itself is short.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Matching what the teacher computes inside: hints, attention, states
md: Feature losses need alignment that output losses do not: a projection or regressor when widths differ (FitNets, TinyBERT's W_h), a layer mapping when depths differ, and the same spatial grid or the same token positions. Output distillation needs none of this, only the same set of classes or the same vocabulary.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Eviction trades exactness for a fixed memory budget. Keep the sink tokens, keep recent tokens, and use accumulated attention to keep the heavy hitters; anything evicted cannot be recovered.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Reuse offloading does not make the GPU's attention kernel read from CPU memory. Blocks are copied back into GPU blocks before the kernel runs; the kernel only ever sees HBM. What it buys is skipping the *prefill compute* that would otherwise recreate those blocks. Capacity offloading can differ: FlexGen can run attention on the CPU, where the KV lives.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
md: HLC is still one-way like Lamport: $(l, c)$ ordering never tells you two events are concurrent. Its gain is closeness to real time and constant size, not concurrency detection.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: ColBERT and ColPali are the same idea at different granularities: keep one vector per token or patch, precompute the document side, and let each query token pick its best match.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: A continuous thought can encode a weighted set of next steps. Coconut reached 97.0% on ProsQA where CoT reached 77.5%, generating 14.2 tokens instead of 49.4. The probes suggest deferring commitment is part of why, but staged training without any thoughts also reached 95.5%.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: An RMI separates model size from execution cost. A lookup evaluates exactly one model per stage, however many leaf models exist. Adding leaves makes each leaf's slice smaller and its error bounds tighter without adding work per lookup.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
md: Cost is driven by the total length of the posting lists the query touches, not by vocabulary size. Every extra query expansion term and every long posting list is extra work. That is why sparsity, especially on the query side, is the thing training must control.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: What a fixed state cannot do: recall limits and state tracking
md: Do not mix the two limits up. A bigger state helps recall but does nothing for parity: with eigenvalues in [0, 1], even a huge state fails at long lengths. Negative eigenvalues fix parity but add no storage. Production models answer the recall limit by keeping some attention layers (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Services, systemd and cron: what runs without anyone logged in
md: A cron job run by root that executes a script writable by another user is a privilege escalation waiting to happen: whoever can edit the script chooses what root runs every night. When auditing, check the permissions of every file a root job calls, not only the crontab line.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise
md: Patch, expose less, use keys, grant little, keep logs off the box and keep baselines. Each step is simple; together they turn most of the attacks in this course from silent root into a noisy, short-lived event.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Kernel lockdown modes and sysctl baselines across a fleet
md: Use lockdown integrity mode on fleets that run eBPF or kprobe sensors; confidentiality also blocks the reads those sensors need. Lockdown only ever goes up until reboot. For sysctl, the last-sorted file wins across directories, so always verify running values, not config files.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
md: A kprobe policy depends on a kernel function name and its arguments, which are not a stable interface and can change between kernel versions. Test policies against every kernel version in your fleet, and watch for the policy failing to load after a kernel update.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: regreSSHion across a fleet, from advisory to verified fix
md: Fleet response = package-aware inventory, immediate exposure reduction through config management, ring rollout with restarts, verification of running code, and detection of the attack's noise in the meantime. Never triage on upstream version strings alone.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
md: Use an LLM judge to label at scale, but never let the measurement and the thing measured share the same model and prompt, and keep a human gold set to check the instrument. When the judge is also a ranking component, its scores stop measuring anything.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
md: Masking the model's input and output does not mask everything else. The AWS docs say Bedrock invocation logs (its record of each model call) keep the original request, and the `match` field of the guardrail trace (the per-request report of what each policy found) contains the original PII value by design. Protect logs and traces separately.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Capacity in sequences is roughly pool bytes / (bytes per token x tokens per sequence). Every lever (GQA, FP8 KV, more GPUs, smaller weights, shorter contexts, less waste per sequence) moves one of those three terms.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a small engine with a block manager
md: An LLM engine is a loop: pick requests under a token budget, ask a block allocator whether each fits, evict when it does not, run one forward pass, sample, repeat. Writing it yourself makes every knob in this course something you can test.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
md: Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA**, short for parsing accuracy, for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
md: Monitor the pipeline like a production service: events per source per hour, parse-failure rate, queue depth, and the age of the newest event. A sensor that stops sending looks exactly like a quiet, safe network. Also alert on deliberate blinding: Windows event 1102 (Security log cleared) and CloudTrail StopLogging or DeleteTrail calls are ATT&CK Defense Impairment techniques (T1685.005, T1685.002).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
md: Use indicators (hashes, IPs, domains) for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history after a report is published. Invest your engineering time in behaviour detections, because they are the ones that still work next month.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Other routes to long context: base scaling, searched factors, data
md: The common production recipe: pick a large RoPE base (or raise it), then continue pretraining on a balanced mix with long documents upsampled, extending length in stages. Llama 3's six stages and 800B tokens (lesson 8) are the large-scale version. Inference-time rescaling (YaRN, Llama 3.1's rule, LongRoPE factors) is layered on top to go further.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
md: Turning a GPT into a recurrent-depth model takes a split into prelude, core and coda, a concat adapter, a noise start and a random-depth training loop. The monitor that matters is the gap between low-r and high-r validation loss.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference
md: Merging has a price: a merged model serves one adapter. Hu et al. note it is not straightforward to batch requests for *different* adapters in one forward pass once A and B are folded into W. Serving many adapters at once needs the unmerged form, which is the subject of the multi-LoRA serving course.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Certified removal: what 'as if retrained' means formally
md: Weights that are close to the retrained weights are not removal. Certified removal is a statement about the *distribution* of models, and it needs randomness added at training time to hide what the leftover error reveals.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Toward robust unlearning: tamper resistance, distillation, filtering
md: Robustness numbers from different papers are not comparable. Each uses its own model, data, attack budget and step definition, and Deep Ignorance itself notes that fine-tuning attack configurations are hard to compare. Compare methods only inside one paper's evaluation, and treat any red-teaming result as a lower bound.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: TCC: consent prompts, the databases and who is asking
md: Granting Full Disk Access to Terminal, an IDE or a remote-management agent is common, and it means anything running under that app can read Mail, Messages and every TCC-protected folder. Inventory which apps hold Full Disk Access across the fleet, and treat a new grant as an event worth reviewing (Endpoint Security reports `tcc_modify`).

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
